title: Swapping with Jeter-Pillars for a Black club across town
summary: The managers trade bands so Eckstine's group plays a Black club with a chorus line for four weeks.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Anyway, it was the next day that the manager made an agreement with a club across town, which was a Black club that Jeter-Pillars had gone into for the month that we were going to be in the Plantation Club. So the manager of the club made a pact with the Black clubowner to let us go in his club and let Jeter-Pillars come back to The Plantation. Which was very agreeable with everybody, including us, because we were very tight in there. After we came down off the bandstand, we had to go outside or in the dressing room somewhere. You couldn't stay in the club, you couldn't have a drink or nothing like that.
So it was agreed, and the club-owner at the Plantation paid our salary while we worked in this other club, and of course, vice-versa. And for the rest of the four weeks, we

just had a beautiful time in St. Louis, and we worked there... The other club was a large club, too, a good club. It had a Black chorus line in there, a girl named Hortense Allen, who became quite a dancer, who was quite a dancer, and she had a chorus line. It was a very, very good show. And we just had a real ball for the next four weeks there. We rehearsed and got our repertoire together, and this allowed things to develop, because when a band can sit in one place for a while you can get things together, you can kind of get settled, you know.
